subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Which of these is a compound?
items.note: A compound has two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. O₂ is an element; air and brass (an alloy) are mixtures.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Which technique separates the dyes in a sample of ink?
items.note: Components travel different distances depending on their attraction to the paper vs solubility in the solvent.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Which change of state is exothermic?
items.note: Energy is released when attractions form between particles (freezing, condensation, deposition).

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Doubling the absolute temperature of a gas doubles:
choices: The average kinetic energy of its particles
The average speed of the particles, since kinetic energy is proportional to speed
items.note: Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature. Speed increases by √2, not 2.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: During boiling of a pure liquid, the temperature stays constant because:
choices: Energy is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to increase kinetic energy
The liquid stops absorbing energy from the heat source once it reaches its boiling point and begins to bubble
Particles lose kinetic energy as they become a gas
Bonds within the molecules are broken
items.note: The energy supplied separates particles (latent heat). Covalent bonds within molecules are not broken.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Which mixture is best separated by simple distillation?
items.note: Distillation separates a volatile solvent from dissolved solids. Use filtration for sand; a separating funnel for immiscible liquids; a magnet for iron.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: A heating curve of a pure substance has a horizontal section for melting that is much shorter than the one for boiling. This is because:
choices: Melting happens at a lower temperature, so less heat is supplied
More energy is needed to separate particles completely into a gas
The substance has a higher specific heat capacity as a solid
Covalent bonds break during boiling but not melting
items.note: Boiling separates particles fully against all remaining attractions; melting only loosens them.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Which state symbol equation represents sublimation of iodine?
items.note: Sublimation = solid directly to gas. The reverse (g → s) is deposition.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: In a mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (100 °C), fractional distillation works because:
choices: Ethanol vapour reaches the top of the column first, as it has the lower boiling point
Water evaporates first because it has stronger forces
The two liquids are immiscible and form separate layers
Ethanol freezes at a higher temperature than water
items.note: Repeated condensation and evaporation in the column enrich the more volatile component in the vapour.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Which statement about a heterogeneous mixture is correct?
choices: It has a uniform composition throughout
It has a non-uniform composition, with visibly different parts
It is always a solution of a solid in a liquid
items.note: Heterogeneous mixtures (e.g. sand in water) have distinct phases; homogeneous mixtures (solutions) are uniform.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Describe, in terms of particles, what happens when ice melts.
markscheme: Energy is absorbed by the particles (1)
Particles vibrate more and overcome some of the intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) (1)
Particles move from fixed positions to moving past each other, still close together (1)

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Outline how to obtain pure, dry salt crystals from a mixture of salt and sand.
markscheme: Add water and stir to dissolve the salt (1)
Evaporate/heat the filtrate to crystallise the salt, then dry (1)
items.tactic: Separation sequences: one technique per step, in order.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem: Explain why the temperature of a pure substance stays constant while it changes state, even though it is being heated.
markscheme: Energy supplied is used to overcome attractions between particles (1)
Average kinetic energy of the particles does not increase (1)
Temperature measures average kinetic energy, so it stays constant (1)
items.tactic: Link temperature to kinetic energy explicitly.

items.topicLabel: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A pure substance was heated at a constant rate. Temperature (°C) every minute from 0 to 10 min: −20, −8, 4, 5, 5, 5, 20, 41, 62, 80, 80.
(a) State the melting point. (b) Estimate the boiling point. (c) Identify the state of the substance at 7 min. (d) Explain how the data show that the substance is pure.
markscheme: (d) Sharp, constant melting temperature (plateau) rather than melting over a range (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
